title: Tail, Head and Indirect Recursion
quickIdea: Name the shape before you answer: tail (the call is the last action), head (the call comes first), tree (several calls), nested (a call inside an argument), indirect (a cycle of functions).
remember: Tail recursion: the recursive call is the last operation and its result is returned unchanged, so nothing remains to be done when it returns.
Head recursion: the call comes first and the work happens on the unwinding - the digit and character printers of the previous cards are head recursions, which is exactly why they reverse the output.
Tree recursion: more than one call per activation. Nested recursion: a recursive call appears as an argument of another call, as in Ackermann's function.

Indirect (mutual) recursion: f calls g and g calls f. Termination then needs an argument that decreases across the whole cycle, not inside one function, and a compiler cannot as easily turn the cycle into a loop.
The costs the standard treatment states: tail and head recursion are O(n) time and O(n) space; tree recursion is O(2^n) time with O(n) space.
The shape decides both what GATE can ask - the order of the output, the count of the calls - and what an optimiser can do with the code.

example.prompt: Classify each of these: (a) int f(int n) { return n == 0 ? 1 : n * f(n-1); } (b) int g(int n, int acc) { return n == 0 ? acc : g(n-1, acc*n); } (c) void h(int n) { if (n == 0) return; h(n-1); printf("%d", n); }
example.work: (a) has the multiplication after the call, so work remains on the return: head-style linear recursion, not a tail call. (b) returns the result of the call unchanged and carries the accumulator in a parameter: a tail call. (c) prints after the call, so the work happens on the unwinding: head recursion.
example.answer: (a) linear recursion with work on the unwind, (b) tail recursion, (c) head recursion.

gateAngle: No GATE CSE question of the last decade asks 'what kind of recursion is this'; the shape is tested through its consequences, as an output order (2024 Set 1 Q.19) or a call count (2015 Set 3 Q.39). Learn the names because they make those consequences predictable, not because they are asked directly.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: In fun(k) * fun(n-k) from GATE CSE 2015 Set 2 Q.11, which shape is the recursion, and what does that predict about its cost?
variations.answer: Tree recursion with a branching factor that grows with n; the call count is exponential in n, which is why the question is answered by tabulation rather than by expansion.
variations.why: Connects the taxonomy to the cost, which is what the paper actually tests.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why can a head recursion not be rewritten as a loop by simply moving the statement?
variations.answer: Because the work depends on the frame that is still alive: the print of frame k must happen after the whole subtree below it. A loop would have to carry that pending work in an explicit stack.
variations.why: This is the reason tail-call elimination works only for tail calls, and the reason recursion is worth having at all.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Two functions f and g call each other, with f(n) = g(n-1) and g(n) = f(n-1), base f(0) = 0. Does f(5) terminate?
variations.answer: Yes: the argument decreases by 1 on every call of either function, so the cycle reaches the base case after five steps.
variations.why: Mutual recursion terminates on a measure that falls across the cycle, not necessarily inside one function.

trap.what: Calling any recursion with a statement after the call 'tail recursion'.
trap.why: Tail position means nothing is left to do with the result. A printf after the call, or a multiplication by the returned value, leaves work in the frame, so the frame cannot be discarded.
trap.counterexample: int f(int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; printf("%d", n); return n * f(n-1); } looks like it ends with a call but the multiplication follows it, so it is not a tail call.

check.question: Which of these is a tail call? int a(int n) { return n == 0 ? 0 : 1 + a(n-1); } or int b(int n, int s) { return n == 0 ? s : b(n-1, s+n); }
check.explanation: In a the returned value is 1 plus the result of the call, so the addition happens after the call returns; in b the result of the call is returned unchanged.
